questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation
questions.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T$ that maps the $uvw$-space into the $xyz$-space by means of the equations

$$
x=u\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +v\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,y=v\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -u\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=w.
$$

You may assume that $\theta $ is a fixed constant.
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation
questions.problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} \\ {e}^{x+y} \\ {e}^{x+y+z}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)={e}^{x},\,v(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y},\,w(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & ={e}^{x} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & ={e}^{x+y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & ={e}^{x+y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={e}^{x+y+z} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & ={e}^{x+y+z} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & ={e}^{x+y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & 0 & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y} & {e}^{x+y} & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{x}|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+y} & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{x}({e}^{2x+2y+z}-0) \\  & ={e}^{3x+2y+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{3x+2y+z} & ={e}^{x+(x+y)+(x+y+z)} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot {e}^{x+y+z} \\  & =uvw\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{uvw}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation
questions.problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}y{z}^{2} \\ z{x}^{2} \\ x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z\ne 0.$*
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=y{z}^{2},\,v(x,y,z)=z{x}^{2},\,w(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & ={z}^{2} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2yz \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2xz & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & ={x}^{2} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={y}^{2} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2xy & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & {z}^{2} & 2yz \\ 2xz & 0 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-{z}^{2}|\begin{aligned}2xy & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 0\end{aligned}|+2yz|\begin{aligned}2xz & 0 \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy\end{aligned}| \\  & =-{z}^{2}(0-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})+2yz(4{x}^{2}yz-0) \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} \\  & =9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} & =9{({x}^{3}{y}^{3}{z}^{3})}^{2/3} \\  & =9{(y{z}^{2}\cdot z{x}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2})}^{2/3} \\  & =9(uvw)^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9(uvw)^{2/3}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Critical Points of a Transformation
questions.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+2w \\ v-u \\ uw\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+2w,\,y(u,v,w)=v-u,\,z(u,v,w)=uw.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =2 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =w & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ w & 0 & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =1|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & u\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ w & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(u-0)+2(0-w) \\  & =u-2w.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ u-2w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u-2w=0$ defines the plane $u=2w.$

choices.value: The critical points lie on the plane $u=2w.$
The critical points lie on the plane $u+v-2w=0.$
The critical points lie on the $vw-$ plane.
The critical points lie on the elliptic cylinder ${u}^{2}+2{w}^{2}=1.$
The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $v={u}^{2}.$

answer_fields.correct_value: The critical points lie on the plane $u=2w.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Critical Points of a Transformation
questions.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{u} \\ vw \\ u+w\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=\sqrt{u},\,y(u,v,w)=vw,\,z(u,v,w)=u+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =v \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & w & v \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}|\begin{aligned}w & v \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ w & v\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}(w-0)+0 \\  & =\frac{w}{2\sqrt{u}}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ \frac{w}{2\sqrt{u}} & =0 \\ w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $w=0$ defines the plane $w=0,$ i.e., $uv$-plane.

choices.value: The critical points lie on the sphere ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+{w}^{2}=2.$
The critical points lie on the $uv-$plane.
The critical points lie on the plane $u=w.$
The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $v={w}^{2}.$
The critical points lie on the $vw-$plane.

answer_fields.correct_value: The critical points lie on the $uv-$plane.
